name: Acetazolamide (Diamox)
lead: Acetazolamide, sold under the brand name Diamox among others, is a sulfonamide-derived carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that increases the kidney's excretion of bicarbonate, sodium and water. It is an older prescription drug used for glaucoma, certain edemas, some seizure disorders and the prevention of acute mountain sickness. [1][2]

In appearance-focused communities it is listed under "depuffing" because it is a diuretic that reduces fluid in the body. The wiki found no published study that has tested acetazolamide for facial puffiness, facial water retention or any cosmetic outcome, and no community discussion of the drug was available to document. [1]

Its studied uses are medical: a randomized trial in acute decompensated heart failure examined it as an add-on to loop diuretics, and a trial in idiopathic intracranial hypertension examined it for protecting vision. [3][4] Labelled adverse effects include metabolic acidosis, electrolyte disturbances, paresthesia and rare, sometimes fatal sulfonamide-type reactions. [2]

paras: The US label lists adjunctive treatment of edema due to congestive heart failure and drug-induced edema, centrencephalic epilepsies, chronic open-angle and secondary glaucoma, and preoperative lowering of eye pressure in acute angle-closure glaucoma. It is also labelled for preventing or easing symptoms of acute mountain sickness. [2]
Off-label uses described in reference works include idiopathic intracranial hypertension, periodic paralysis, central sleep apnea and metabolic alkalosis in critical care. [1]

Carbonic anhydrase is a zinc-containing enzyme that catalyses the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide to bicarbonate and a proton. [7] Acetazolamide inhibits the enzyme, which in the kidney's proximal tubule reduces reabsorption of bicarbonate, sodium and water, producing a mild diuresis and a metabolic acidosis. [1] The same enzyme inhibition reduces aqueous humor formation in the eye. [1]

The label lists headache, fatigue, gastrointestinal upset, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte imbalance including low potassium and sodium, and rare blood disorders and liver injury. [2] It carries a warning that fatalities have occurred, rarely, from severe sulfonamide-type reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. [2]
Animal studies have shown limb defects with acetazolamide, and there are no adequate controlled studies in pregnant women, according to the label. [2]

Grokipedia attributes the synthesis of acetazolamide to Richard O. Roblin Jr. and James W. Clapp at Lederle Laboratories in the 1940s, with pharmacological work by Thomas H. Maren, and states that the US FDA approved it in 1953. [1]
No studies found on acetazolamide for facial puffiness or cosmetic depuffing. Studies exist only for its medical indications.

In the ADVOR randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in 2022, acetazolamide was tested as an add-on to loop diuretics in patients hospitalised with acute decompensated heart failure and volume overload. [3] The Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Treatment Trial (JAMA, 2014) evaluated acetazolamide on visual function in people with mild visual loss. [4] An observational study of 278 hikers in Nepal in 1976 examined the incidence of acute mountain sickness and its prophylaxis, and a later Lancet review covers high-altitude illness. [5][6] A phase 4 trial has examined dosing for obstructive sleep apnea. [8]

card.summary: A sulfonamide carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used for glaucoma, edema and altitude sickness; it is a diuretic, but nothing shows it reduces facial puffiness.
card.note: Prescription drug with rare serious sulfonamide-type reactions; no appearance studies.

quick.overview:
Acetazolamide (Diamox) is an older prescription diuretic that blocks the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. Doctors use it for glaucoma, some forms of edema, certain seizure disorders, raised pressure inside the skull and the prevention of altitude sickness.

It is grouped under depuffing because it makes the body shed fluid, but no study has tested it for facial puffiness or any cosmetic goal.
quick.mechanism: By inhibiting carbonic anhydrase, it reduces reabsorption of bicarbonate, sodium and water in the kidney and lowers fluid production in the eye, causing mild diuresis and a metabolic acidosis.
quick.risks: The label lists tingling, fatigue, stomach upset, acid-base and electrolyte disturbances, and rare, sometimes fatal sulfonamide-type reactions and blood disorders. It is prescription-only in the US and carries a pregnancy caution based on animal limb defects.
